lower-0862-s9-test-a-claim.description: Use totals, ordered outcomes and scale factors to justify conclusions across topics.

sections.title: Whose visits count in the mean?
sections.label: Combine counts
sections.intro: Start with each group’s total. If you are given a group mean, recovering its total shows how much each group contributes.

blocks.html: A combined mean is the sum of the group totals divided by the combined headcount. A larger group has more weight.

figure.alt: One group of four people and another group of nine.
figure.caption: A person in either group counts once. Use the group sizes to combine group means.

blocks.prompt:
The table gives the numbers of library visits made by the members of two clubs.

ClubMembersMean visits
North87
South1313

Find the mean number of visits per person for both clubs combined. Give an exact answer.
blocks.hint: Work out the two totals before finding the combined mean.
blocks.solution:
Find the two totals. The North total is 8 times 7. The South total is 13 times 13.

Together there are 225 visits and 21 people. Divide visits by people.

\(\frac{75}{7}\)

retry.feedback: The clubs have different sizes. Add all visits and divide by all the people.

blocks.html: An ordinary mean of the two group means gives equal weight to the groups. Check whether their sizes match before doing that.

sections.title: Which outcomes belong to the event?
sections.label: Test both orders
sections.intro: List possible two-draw routes first. Mark every order that fits what the question asks. If the first object is kept, update the counts for the second draw.

blocks.html: For one route, multiply its consecutive probabilities. Add the probabilities of separate routes that can each give the event.

figure.alt: The two possible colours on each of two draws give BB, BW, WB and WW.
figure.caption: BW and WB have different orders. Add their probabilities to count one of each colour.

blocks.prompt:
A bag holds 3 blue counters and 8 white counters. Two counters are drawn one after the other. The first counter is kept out of the bag.

Find the probability of getting one counter of each colour, in either order.
blocks.hint: Multiply along each order and then add the probabilities for both orders.
blocks.solution:
List the orders BW and WB. The first draw is from 11 counters. The second draw is from 10 counters.

Each order has probability \(\frac{12}{55}\). Add the two probabilities.

\(\frac{24}{55}\)

retry.feedback: Your calculation gives one order. Include both BW and WB.

blocks.html: Writing down only blue then white misses white then blue. Writing the same fractions for both stages misses the removal.

blocks.html: Label your order. After the first draw, check the new total before setting the second denominator.

sections.title: Which measurements scale twice?
sections.label: Choose a factor
sections.intro: Sketch matching rectangles and mark the scaled side lengths. Count how many copies of the original area fit when both dimensions grow.

blocks.html: Perimeter uses the length scale factor. For area, each of the two dimensions contributes one factor, so the multiplier is its square.

figure.alt: A rectangle is doubled in both directions and contains four copies of the original area.
figure.caption: Doubling both lengths gives four original areas.

blocks.prompt:
A rectangular design is 12 cm by 18 cm. A larger copy is made with length scale factor \(4\).

Find the area of the larger design in square centimetres.
blocks.hint: Square the length scale factor to get the area scale factor.
blocks.solution:
Both side lengths are multiplied by \(4\). The area is multiplied by \(16\).

The old area is 216 square centimetres. Multiply it by the area factor.

\(3456\) square centimetres

retry.feedback: The factor is applied to both dimensions. Multiply the original area by the square of the factor.

blocks.html: Multiplying the area by the length factor stretches only one dimension. An enlargement changes both dimensions.

retry.feedback: The factor is applied to both dimensions. Multiply the original area by the square of the factor.

blocks.html: Name the quantity before choosing its multiplier. State length or area units with the answer.

examples.title: Combining two groups fairly
examples.question:
The table gives the numbers of library visits made by the members of two clubs.

ClubMembersMean visits
North83
South1113

  1. Find the mean number of visits per person for both clubs combined. Give an exact answer.

    [2]

  2. Find the total number of visits by members of the larger club.

    [2]

  3. One member changes clubs but keeps the same number of visits. Explain what happens to the combined mean.

    [2]
solution: (a) Find the two totals. The North total is 8 times 3. The South total is 11 times 13.
Together there are 167 visits and 19 people. Divide visits by people.
(b) Each member contributes 13 visits on average. Multiply by 11 members.
(c) The move changes the groups. The inputs to the combined mean stay fixed.
It stays the same. The total number of visits and the total number of people are unchanged.

examples.title: Two draws without replacement
examples.question:
A bag holds 4 blue counters and 5 white counters. Two counters are drawn one after the other. The first counter is kept out of the bag.

  1. Find the probability of getting one counter of each colour, in either order.

    [2]

  2. Find the probability of two blue counters.

    [2]

  3. Explain why the probability of blue usually changes between the first and second draws.

    [2]
solution: (a) List the orders BW and WB. The first draw is from 9 counters. The second draw is from 8 counters.
Each order has probability \(\frac{5}{18}\). Add the two probabilities.
(b) After drawing one blue counter, there are 3 blue counters left out of 8.
(c) The first draw determines which counts are used in the fraction for the second draw.
One counter has been removed. If it was blue, both the number of blue counters and the total fall. If it was white, only the total falls.

examples.title: A larger copy of a display
examples.question:
A rectangular design is 12 cm by 16 cm. A larger copy is made with length scale factor \(3\).

  1. Find the area of the larger design in square centimetres.

    [2]

  2. Find the perimeter of the larger design in centimetres.

    [2]

  3. Explain why the same multiplier cannot be used for both perimeter and area.

    [2]
solution: (a) Both side lengths are multiplied by \(3\). The area is multiplied by \(9\).
The old area is 192 square centimetres. Multiply it by the area factor.
\(1728\) square centimetres
(b) The perimeter is a length. Multiply the original perimeter 56 cm by \(3\) once.
(c) Writing each calculation using the two side lengths shows how often the scale factor appears.
The perimeter adds scaled lengths. The area multiplies two scaled lengths, so the factor occurs twice.

examples.title: A larger copy of a display
examples.question:
A rectangular design is 3 cm by 8 cm. A larger copy is made with length scale factor \(3\).

  1. Find the area of the larger design in square centimetres.

    [2]

  2. Find the perimeter of the larger design in centimetres.

    [2]

  3. Explain why the same multiplier cannot be used for both perimeter and area.

    [2]
solution: (a) Both side lengths are multiplied by \(3\). The area is multiplied by \(9\).
The old area is 24 square centimetres. Multiply it by the area factor.
\(216\) square centimetres
(b) The perimeter is a length. Multiply the original perimeter 22 cm by \(3\) once.
(c) Writing each calculation using the two side lengths shows how often the scale factor appears.
The perimeter adds scaled lengths. The area multiplies two scaled lengths, so the factor occurs twice.
